title: VOIAJOR — Voyager 1 and 2, from launch into the far future
desc: A detailed simulation of the trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2, from 1977 to over a billion years from now, at any scale.

ev.v1.jup: Closest pass: ≈349,000 km from the planet's center. Discovers the volcanism on Io.
ev.v1.sat: ≈124,000 km. Flies past Titan; the trajectory rises above the plane of the planets.

ev.v1.ts: ≈94 AU: the solar wind abruptly slows down.
ev.v1.hp: ≈121.6 AU: the first probe to enter interstellar space.
ev.v2.launch: Launched 16 days before Voyager 1, on a slower trajectory.
ev.v2.ura: ≈81,500 km. The only visit by a probe.
ev.v2.nep: ≈4,950 km above the clouds; then Triton. The trajectory dips south.
ev.v2.hp: ≈119 AU: the second probe in interstellar space, with a working plasma instrument.

ev.sil.x: The plutonium generators lose ≈4 W per year; instruments shut down one by one, and the probes end up without transmission. Rough dating.

ap.note: Literature: NASA/JPL, via Wikipedia. Over light-year distances, an error of a few degrees in a probe's direction of motion changes the minimum distance by tenths of a light-year or more (for Sirius, over two light-years), so the model's values are only indicative.
ab.p1: The paths of the two Voyager probes from 1977 to a future up to 1 billion years away, at any scale: from Earth's orbit to the disk of the Milky Way. The 1 light-day circle (≈173 AU) is the milestone Voyager 1 is heading towards in 2026–2027.
ab.p2: Planets: mean Keplerian orbital elements (JPL, valid 1800–2050). Until 5 Nov 2026: ballistic arcs (heliocentric conics, the Lambert problem) from launch to each planet, on the actual flyby dates; gravity assists appear as sudden changes of speed at the planet. Then a straight line with solar gravitational deceleration, calibrated to reach the position of 5 Nov 2026. After 2026: inertial motion plus the Sun's correction, and over the long term the Galaxy's pull through the epicyclic (Hill) equations with Oort constants A=15.3 and B=−11.9 km/s/kpc and a vertical frequency of ≈0.08 rad/Myr. Stars: J2000 positions, parallax, proper motion and approximate radial velocity, propagated with the same dynamics.
ab.p3: The 2026 positions (distance, direction) are approximations; at light-year scales they differ from JPL ephemerides. No pull from other bodies and no trajectory corrections; planetary flybys are treated as points (patched conics). The galactic model is a linearization around the Sun's orbit: accurate over tens of millions of years, indicative from hundreds of millions of years onward, when the probes are kiloparsecs from the Sun. The dates for the end of transmission are estimates, not official predictions.
ab.p4: On start-up the app syncs with the device clock (“Real time” mode): relative dates (“ago”, “in”) and the “today” marker on the path refer to today. The probes' position is extrapolated from the last calibrated position (5 Nov 2026), valid for any later date; the “Now” button returns to real time at any moment.
ab.p5: The “📅 Date” button opens a window where you can pick an exact calendar date (time in UTC, from the launches to +1 billion years), an interval relative to today (“in 250 years”, “10 years ago”) or a quick moment. After you choose, “Play” continues from there, at 1 year per second. The page address gets a #t= marker that can be saved or sent.
ab.p6: Drag on the screen to rotate, wheel / pinch to zoom (this turns off auto-zoom), double-click to reset the angle. Space = play / pause. The “co-rotating” frame shows the path in the system that rotates with the Galaxy.
ab.p7: Each probe carries a gold-plated copper disc with sounds and images of Earth, as a message for a possible discovery in the very distant future.
ab.src: Mission data source: NASA/JPL. A single-file app that works without internet.
